title: We die daily
hook: each day a little of life is taken from us (Letters 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was real joy, the serious, steady kind. Your line was learn how to feel joy.
screen: `REAL JOY — LEARN HOW TO FEEL JOY.`

segments.voice: Lucilius is anxious. An enemy is threatening him with a lawsuit, and he has written to Seneca about how it might turn out. The twenty-fourth letter talks him through the fear. Then, near the end, Seneca reaches for a simple object: the clepsydra, a water clock, a vessel that marks time as the water runs out of it. And he turns it on the whole of a life.
screen: `AN ENEMY THREATENS A LAWSUIT.` → `SENECA TALKS HIM THROUGH IT.` → `THE WATER CLOCK, TURNED ON A LIFE.`

segments.voice: In Latin, cotidie morimur: we die every day. Seneca explains at once. Every day, some part of life is taken away. Even while we're growing up, life is shrinking. We lost childhood, then youth, and every yesterday up to this one. This very day we're dividing with death. It isn't the last drop that empties the clepsydra, he says, but everything that flowed out before it. The final hour doesn't make death. It only finishes it. Why say something this bleak to a frightened friend? Because it shrinks the fear. If dying is something we've been doing quietly every day, the last day is less of a monster: the end of a long, ordinary process, not an ambush. Seneca also warns against the opposite mistake. Some people grow so tired of living that they long for death. He wants neither terror nor weariness, just clear sight. If this day is being spent whether you notice or not, the question isn't whether to spend it. It's how. It's the same thread as the first letter's three thieves, seen from the other side. Not a reason for gloom. A reason to look up from the screen and notice the water running.
screen: `COTIDIE MORIMUR: WE DIE EVERY DAY.` · `NOT THE LAST DROP EMPTIES THE CLOCK.` · `NEITHER TERROR NOR WEARINESS.` · `TODAY IS BEING SPENT. HOW?` · then, large: `WE DIE DAILY.`

segments.voice: Sit still and listen to whatever is ticking: a clock, your heartbeat, your breath going in and out. Let a few breaths pass and count them, each one a drop from the vessel, not frightening, just true. Then ask gently, without judgment, what this day is being spent on.
Cotidie morimur. Latin for we die every day: the last hour only finishes what's been happening all along. Today's word.
Your line: notice the water running. Neither terror nor weariness, just clear sight. Day four hundred fifty-four, done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners pause during the day to remember that time is passing, and use that reminder to choose what the next hour is for.
